title: S on X: "GTA 6 is the last studio AAA-release. Ever. The industry’s business model has been cooked for years
author: Jonesiller5383
selftext:
The post: [https://x.com/Rubzem/status/2123084499496079783?a=H8BjWVe7bYfIeFMpG5w&s=20](https://x.com/Rubzem/status/2123084499496079783?a=H8BjWVe7bYfIeFMpG5w&s=20)  
  
Awesome thought piece about the game industry and making games with AI. So worth a read.  
  
**Some of my favorite parts:**

We get a new Madden, NBA, FC, or COD every year. Same game. New price tag. More ways to squeeze you.

Or we wait a decade for the next GTA or Elder Scrolls because a new game might threaten the cash cow the old one became.

Thousands of employees. Endless production cycles. Budgets so big you can’t afford a weird idea.

Meanwhile, a solo dev with AI can finally build something they’ve dreamed about for years. 

My bet: the next renaissance in games comes from solo devs and tiny teams embracing AI. People who can afford to make something strange, fail, and try again.

  
Do you agree with the post?

replies.author: MaxwellHowl
replies.body:
Yeah.  This is so stupid.  No one has made anything close to a AAA game with vibe coding.  It can make fun little indie games and casual games.  AAA games are a whole different beast.  

What AI is going to do is save AAA games.  They are going to bring down team sizes and development times, and make it much easier to be profitable. Piracy may go up thanks to AI and people decomping and emulating, but that was never a big scene.  Most people just buy cool AAA games.

I am doing AI game dev myself.  I love it.  It's the most fun I've had as a game dev in a long time.  But this kind of post is so silly.

replies.author: AdminClown
replies.body:
Exactly. The same way that it works as force multiplier and enabler for normal people and indie devs, it does for AAA studios.

It has enabled fantastic things to be done by people that would otherwise not have the means. But it can't fix stupid and uninspired, and unfortunately that is all over the place here .

replies.author: anon999387
replies.body: The capable models are not even a few months old...you're underestimating what is coming.

replies.author: HaMMeReD
replies.body:
It depends on what you are doing really. Are you making a game, or are you automating the process of making a game.

The mindshare that small projects need to take isn't just using AI to do the traditional work, it's how do you decompose the entire process with AI.

Games are largely content, if you build effective content pipelines, you can make big games. AI is just scratching the surface of that today, but it's getting pretty close.

replies.author: TheFlyingSheeps
replies.body: Turns out making a game is still a shit ton of work. You can get a nice loop done quickly but that leaves the plot and everything else that needs to come together

replies.author: HaMMeReD
replies.body:
Having a view from both sides of the fence here.

Large organizations are entrenched. So while they have more AI resources available to them, they refuse the full agility/risk that indies can afford.

For example in my big-tech day-job I have a ton of AI can leverage it to really advanced things really quickly, but if I want to actually deliver a feature, even an internal engineering effort. It's like dragging weights behind you. There are more people resisting change vs embracing it.

As an indie, you can fully embrace. You don't look at things through the lens of approvals and design docs, you look through the lens of maximizing efficiency and automation with AI. It ends up a very different organization structure and process.

comments.author: monsterfurby
comments.body:
Having worked in the games industry, I've long said that game development budgets have been brutally overextended past any reason in the same way as Hollywood's film productions. The arms race of the 2010s has made the business model of most publishers untenable without cutting corners and engaging in business practices bordering on the unethical.

But at the same time, brands still hold loyalty. IPs hold loyalty. The perfect outcome would be major studios and publishers reorienting towards core strengths and long-term perspectives, while indie dream-projects gives us even more variety and new takes on genres (Steam is currently getting a ton of actually good GenAI-assisted games). I would love a Warcraft IV that's made with the same care as Warcraft III was. I'd love to see a CoD that's more like the Tom Clancy-meets-Action-Schlock fever dream of the original two Modern Warfares' single player campaigns; but to get there, major publishers will need to go for more moderately-sized projects of higher quality and not churn through staff every time a game releases.

Is that going to happen? I don't know. I sure would hope so.

comments.author: mozfromtheblock
comments.body:
The biggest mistake these studios can make is thinking AI gives them an even bigger competitive advantage when it actually destroys the advantage they built their entire business models around.  
For decades, their moat was money: the ability to hire hundreds or thousands of people to build what smaller teams couldn’t afford to build.

AI is dismantling that moat.  
And while they’re celebrating how much they can save by replacing people with AI, they’re overlooking the bigger picture: the same tools are putting capabilities worth millions of dollars into the hands of a developer with a laptop and $100–$200 a month.

comments.author: apf6
comments.body:
ridiculous and false claim.

> Thousands of employees. Endless production cycles. Budgets so big you can’t afford a weird idea.

GTA6 is expected to bring in $5 billion revenue. It warrants the team size. They already know what their customers want, they don't want 'weird' ideas. Their business model is fine.

And if you think small teams with AI are going to compete with those AAA games, just look at the level of quality of those, and then look at how janky and shoddy all the AI-heavy games look. GTA6 level quality is outright unachieveable for AI and will be for at least a few years to come.

> My bet: the next renaissance in games comes from solo devs and tiny teams embracing AI. People who can afford to make something strange, fail, and try again.

it sounds like the author has very little exposure to the indie game world? Indie developers have already been shipping strange and experimental games for decades. There's no lack of people trying experimental ideas. "Passionate game making" never left.

comments.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
comments.body: This is true. There won't be a GTA 7 as we know it. I'd wager GTA 6 will be the last of its kind. Future games like it will be smaller in scale, with around 20-30 people working on them, taking about a year to release. Meanwhile, we'll see hundreds of smaller teams, working remotely and independently, creating games with AI. Many veteran game developers, out of work due to industry changes, are now doing this too. The result? A flood of games hitting the market. Expect some to blow your mind, created by just a handful of people in a short time. The traditional AAA release model is dying. AI's role will only grow, and the "AI slop" criticism will fade.
